notes.s: How quickly the rotary positions turn: the fastest pair 1 radian per patch, the slowest once in 353 patches.
notes.d: 2-D RoPE turns pairs of a query’s and a key’s numbers by angles that grow with the place. Of each head’s 32 numbers, 8 pairs turn with the row and 8 with the column; pair i turns ROPE_BASE ** (-i / 8) radians per patch: 1, 0.562, 0.316, 0.178, 0.1, 0.0562, 0.0316, 0.0178.
notes.a: A clock’s hands: the fast one tells nearby moments apart, the slow one moments far apart.
notes.w: Fast pairs tell neighbouring patches apart; slow ones change a little across the whole picture without coming round again, so far-apart places stay different too. The picture is 36 patches wide, so the slowest pair does not even turn once across it.

cap.kernel_size: A 3 × 3 window: each output is the sum of 9 products, weight × number, for each input map. Here a made-up “right minus left” filter on a made-up 6 × 6 map: it gives the most, 25, where the right of its window is brighter than the left. Click an output, or step with ◂ ▸.
cap.stride: The window jumps 2 places, so neighbouring windows share 1 row or column, and the 6 × 6 map gives 3 × 3 outputs; with stride 1 it would give 6 × 6. In the model each step halves the map: 192 × 288 → 96 × 144 → 48 × 72 → 24 × 36.
cap.padding: One ring of zeros: the 6 × 6 map becomes 8 × 8, so a window centred on an edge number fits. The corner window reads 5 zeros, the next one along the top 3. With stride 2, the bottom row and the right column of zeros are never read. Without padding: 2 × 2 here, and the stem would end at 23 × 35, not 24 × 36. conv1’s pixels are normalised first, the average colour subtracted, so there a zero stands for the average colour, not black.
cap.bias: No + b. BatchNorm, right after, subtracts each channel’s mean, so a bias added here would be taken away again: adding 3 to every output moves the mean from 10 to 13 and leaves each output minus the mean the same. 2-D RoPE.d: Rotary positions in two directions: inside attention, half of each query’s and key’s pairs of numbers are turned by the row, half by the column, so a score depends on how far apart two places are, not where they are.

BatchNorm.d: Batch normalisation: keeps each channel’s outputs at a steady size by scaling them with averages over the batch (while training) and with running averages (afterwards).

RoPE.d: Rotary position embedding: pairs of numbers are turned by an angle that grows with the token’s position.

Vision Transformer.d: A Transformer that reads a picture: the picture is cut into patches, and each patch plays the part a word plays in a sentence. Often shortened to ViT.

adamw.d: The optimizer: it keeps a running average of each parameter’s gradient and of its square, and steps each parameter by its own adapted amount; the W adds weight decay, a gentle pull of every weight towards 0.
adamw.a: A hiker who remembers the recent slope under each foot and lengthens or shortens the stride for each leg separately.

affine transform.d: Moving, zooming, mirroring or turning a picture with one small matrix — every point is mapped the same way.

affine-grid.d: A 2 × 3 matrix per picture says where each output pixel should read from in the source (zoom, mirror, shift); affine_grid turns it into coordinates, grid_sample reads the source there. A whole batch is moved in one call.
affine-grid.a: A slide projector you can zoom, flip and aim, for a stack of slides at once.

anywidget.d: A small library for notebook widgets: a Python class with synced attributes (traits), plus a JavaScript module (_esm) and a stylesheet (_css) that the notebook runs in the browser. The two sides share the traits and can send each other messages.
anywidget.a: A walkie-talkie between the Python kernel and the page: either side can change the shared values or call the other.

argmax.d: The position of the largest value: logits.argmax(0) gives, for every pixel, the class with the larger score.
argmax.a: Pointing at the tallest person in the room.

arrow-function.d: (a, b) => a + b is a short function. With braces, x => { … }, it holds several statements. Used here for callbacks: what to do on a click, for each point, and so on.
arrow-function.a: A note saying “when this happens, do that”, written right where it is needed.

attention.d: Each patch gathering information from every other patch, with shares (weights) that add up to 100%.

augmentation.d: Making new training pictures from the ones you have — zoomed, moved, mirrored, recoloured — so a model sees more variety than the photos alone hold.

autograd.d: PyTorch records every operation on tensors that need gradients; loss.backward() walks that record backwards and fills each parameter’s .grad with how the loss changes as it changes.
autograd.a: A trail of breadcrumbs that lets the blame for a mistake be traced back to every dial.

base64.d: Writes bytes as plain text characters, so binary data (a photo) can travel inside JSON or a web page. About a third larger than the bytes.
base64.a: Spelling a picture out in letters to send it by telegram.

batch.d: The examples worked on together in one training step.

bilinear.d: Upsampling that blends the four nearest grid values by how close each is, so the result changes smoothly instead of in blocks.

broadcasting.d: When two tensors of different shapes are combined, axes of size 1 are stretched to match: a (3, 1, 1) mean subtracts from every pixel of a (3, H, W) picture.
broadcasting.a: One instruction read out to the whole class instead of to each pupil.

canvas-2d.d: A <canvas> is a grid of pixels that JavaScript paints with getContext("2d"): paths, fills, strokes, images. What is painted is not a set of elements — to know what was clicked, the code works it out from the coordinates.
canvas-2d.a: An easel: the code paints on it, and nothing painted can be picked up again — only painted over.

cell.d: In Vision v1.5, a 4 × 4-pixel square of the picture: the decoder gives each of the 3,456 cells its two scores.

channel.d: One of a picture’s colour layers — red, green or blue — each a grid of numbers.

checkpoint.d: The parameters saved to a file at some point in training.

class.d: class Name: defines a new kind of object: the data it keeps (attributes, self.x) and the functions that work on it (methods). Name(...) makes one, an instance.
class.a: A blueprint; every house built from it is an instance.

closure.d: A function written inside another keeps the outer function’s variables. Every function inside render shares its photos, people, view, sel and the rest — they live as long as the tool is on screen.
closure.a: A backpack every inner function carries: the variables of the room it was made in.

colab.d: Notebooks that run on Google’s computers. Their disk is wiped when the session ends, so lasting files go on Google Drive, which the notebook mounts as a folder.
colab.a: A borrowed office cleared every evening — keep your papers in your own locker.

composite.d: globalCompositeOperation decides how new paint combines with what is already on the canvas: "source-over" paints on top (the normal way), "destination-out" erases wherever it paints.
composite.a: Turning the brush round to the eraser end — same shape, opposite effect.

comprehension.d: A loop written inside brackets that builds a list, dict or set in one expression: [f(x) for x in xs]. Same result as a for loop that appends, in one line.
comprehension.a: Telling a helper “one of these for each of those” instead of handing items over one by one.

confusion.d: A table counting pixels by (true class, predicted class). The diagonal is what is right; every score — accuracy, IoU — is read off it.
confusion.a: A tally of every answer by what it should have been and what it was.

constant.d: Python has no real constants; a name in CAPITALS tells the reader “set once here, read everywhere, never changed while running”. Changing it here changes the whole run.
constant.a: The numbers written on the recipe card before you start cooking.

conv2d.d: A small learned filter slid over a picture. With a stride as large as the filter, the squares do not overlap, so it becomes one learned matrix applied to each patch.
conv2d.a: A stamp pressed once on every tile of a floor.

convolution.d: A small matrix slid over a picture, applied to one square at a time. With a stride as large as the square, the squares do not overlap: one matrix per patch.

convolutional stem.d: The first layers of the model: small convolutions that turn pixels into patch vectors through windows that overlap, instead of cutting the picture into hard squares.

copy-paste.d: An augmentation for segmentation: cut a labelled object out of one picture and paste it into another, label and all.

cosine decay.d: Lowering the learning rate along half a cosine curve: slowly at first, faster in the middle, gently down to 0 at the end.

cross-attention.d: Attention between two sets: the queries come from one (here the decoder’s cells), the keys and values from the other (the encoder’s patches). The text decoder asks its encoder the same way.

cross-entropy.d: For each pixel: minus the log of the probability the model gave the right class, averaged. 0 when it is certain and right; large when it is sure and wrong.
cross-entropy.a: A fine that grows the more confidently you bet on the wrong horse.

css.d: The rules that say how elements look: selector{property:value;…}. .lt-btn matches every element with that class.
css.a: A style guide: “every heading is bold and dark blue”, written once and applied everywhere.

data-url.d: A whole file written inside a URL as text: data:image/jpeg;base64,…. The photos travel between Python and the browser this way, and an <img> can show one directly.
data-url.a: A letter with the photo printed in the envelope’s address line.

dataloader.d: PyTorch’s way of handing a training loop its batches. With batch_size=None it passes on whatever the dataset yields, already batched.
dataloader.a: The conveyor belt to the oven.

dataset.d: The collection of examples a model learns from and is tested on, each with its label.

decoder.d: The half that writes the answer. In Vision v1.5 every 4 × 4-pixel cell is a query that asks the encoder’s patches what it is (cross-attention); all cells are answered at once, not one by one as the text decoder writes words.

decorator.d: @something on the line above a def hands the function to something, which registers or wraps it. @traitlets.observe("current") registers the method to run whenever current changes.
decorator.a: A sticker on a folder that tells the office what to do with it.

device.d: Where a tensor’s numbers live and are computed: cpu, cuda (an NVIDIA GPU) or mps (an Apple-silicon GPU). Two tensors must be on the same device to be combined; .to(device) moves one.
device.a: Which kitchen the cooking happens in: ingredients have to be in the same kitchen to be mixed.

device-pixel-ratio.d: Screen pixels per CSS pixel — 2 on most sharp laptop screens. A canvas whose pixel grid is that many times larger, shown at its CSS size, draws crisp lines instead of blurry ones.
device-pixel-ratio.a: Drawing on paper twice as fine and shrinking the drawing to fit the frame.

dict.d: A dictionary: values found by a key, d["key"]. dict(a=1) is the same as {"a": 1}.

dom.d: The page is a tree of elements. JavaScript makes one (document.createElement), sets its attributes and text, and hangs it under a parent (appendChild); the browser shows it at once.
dom.a: Building with blocks: make a block, label it, put it on top of another.

dropout.d: While training, sets a random share of the numbers to 0 (and scales the rest up), so the model cannot lean on any one of them. Switched off by model.eval().
dropout.a: Practising with a random team-mate sitting out each round, so nobody becomes indispensable.

dtype.d: The kind of number a tensor holds: float32 for most model numbers, int64 (“long”) for labels and counts, uint8 for image bytes.
dtype.a: Whether a column holds prices, counts or yes/no.

encoder.d: The stack of layers that reads the input. In Vision v1.5 it reads the photo as 864 patches and gives one refined vector per patch: the memory the decoder asks.

epoch.d: One pass over all the training examples.

esm.d: JavaScript that exports what it offers (export default { render }). anywidget imports _esm and calls its render once for every place the widget is shown.
esm.a: A plug with a labelled pin the notebook knows how to plug into.

event-listener.d: el.addEventListener("click", fn) asks the browser to call fn every time that event happens on the element — a click, a key, a wheel turn, a file chosen.
event-listener.a: Leaving your number with the receptionist: they call you when someone arrives.

exif.d: Phones save photos sideways and record the rotation separately; ImageOps.exif_transpose applies it, so the picture is upright as it was shown.
exif.a: Reading the “this way up” arrow on the box before unpacking.

f-string.d: A string with f in front: anything inside {…} is worked out and written in. {x:,} adds thousands separators, {x:.1%} shows a share as a percentage.
f-string.a: A form letter whose blanks fill themselves in.

feed-forward.d: The “think” move: each patch’s vector goes through a small network on its own.

flatten.d: Joins several axes into one: x.flatten(2) turns a grid (B, C, H, W) into a list (B, C, H × W).
flatten.a: Reading a page of rows as one long line.

for-loop.d: Runs its block once for every item of a sequence, with the loop name set to that item each time.
for-loop.a: Going down a list and ticking each line.

from-import.d: Takes only some names out of a module, so the code can write DataLoader instead of torch.utils.data.DataLoader.
from-import.a: Taking two tools out of the box instead of the box.

function.d: def name(args): defines a function: a named block of code that runs only when it is called, with the arguments it is given. return hands a value back.
function.a: A recipe: written once, cooked whenever someone asks.

gelu.d: A smooth bend applied to every number: negative values are mostly let through as almost 0, positive ones almost unchanged. Without a bend, stacked Linear layers would collapse into one.
gelu.a: A gate that opens gradually instead of snapping open.

generalise.d: Do well on pictures a model never saw in training. Learning the training pictures is not the same thing; only a test on unseen pictures measures it.

generator.d: A separate source of random numbers. Giving the DataLoader its own keeps it from taking numbers from the main one, so the training’s random choices stay exactly as they were.
generator.a: A separate deck of cards, so dealing from it does not change the main game’s shuffle.

generator-expression.d: Like a comprehension in round brackets: values are made one at a time as they are asked for, never stored as a list. sum(p.numel() for p in …) adds them up as they come.
generator-expression.a: A tap instead of a bucket.

grad-clip.d: If all gradients together form a vector longer than a limit, shrink them to that length. It stops one unlucky batch from throwing the weights far off.
grad-clip.a: A speed limiter: you can still steer anywhere, just not lurch.

gradient.d: For each parameter, how much the loss would change if the parameter were nudged up a little. The optimizer moves each parameter a step against its gradient.
gradient.a: Which way is downhill, and how steep, for every dial at once.

gradient clipping.d: Shortening the gradient when it is longer than a limit (here 1.0), so one unusual batch cannot throw the weights far off.

head.d: One of several attentions running side by side in a layer; here 4 heads of 32 numbers each.

hit-test.d: Finding what is under the pointer. The canvas has no elements to click, so the code measures the distance from the pointer to every point, edge or shape, and takes the nearest one within a few screen pixels.
hit-test.a: Working out which pin on a map a finger landed on by measuring to each pin.

ignore-index.d: A label value the loss skips entirely: those pixels add nothing to the loss and nothing to the gradient. Here it marks padding, where there is no photo to judge.
ignore-index.a: Leaving a question off the test because it was misprinted.

import.d: Loads a module — a file of ready-made code — and gives it a name in this notebook. import torch.nn as nn loads torch.nn and lets the code call it nn.
import.a: Taking a toolbox off the shelf and putting it on the bench, with a label on the lid.

init.d: The method Python runs when an object is made: it sets the object up. Name(a, b) calls __init__(self, a, b).
init.a: Unpacking and setting up a new appliance before first use.

instance segmentation.d: Telling the objects of one class apart as well: not just “person” but which person — each one gets a number of their own.

integer-division.d: Divides and drops the remainder: 7 // 2 is 3. Used where a count has to be a whole number.
integer-division.a: Cutting a rope into full-length pieces and leaving the scrap.

interpolate.d: Resizes a picture or a grid of scores. bilinear blends the nearest values by distance; nearest copies the closest one; antialias=True averages first when shrinking so thin details do not flicker.
interpolate.a: Enlarging a photocopy, smoothly or in blocks.

iou.d: Intersection over union: pixels both masks call a class, divided by pixels either does. 1 is a perfect match.
iou.a: How much two stencils overlap, out of all the area either covers.

iterable-dataset.d: A PyTorch dataset that produces items as a stream instead of by index — right for pictures made on the fly, where there is no fixed list to number.
iterable-dataset.a: A bakery that bakes to order, as opposed to a shelf of numbered loaves.

json.d: A plain-text format for data — dicts, lists, strings, numbers — that any language can read. json.load turns a file into Python objects, json.dump writes them back.
json.a: A form that every office knows how to fill in.

json-clone.d: JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) writes the data as text and reads it back: a completely new set of arrays and objects with the same values, so changing the copy never changes the original.
json-clone.a: Photocopying a page before writing on it.

key.d: What a patch offers about itself, to be matched against queries.

label.d: The right answer a model learns from. Here: a mask, made by tracing every person by hand.

lambda.d: A small function written in one expression, without a name: lambda x: x * 2.
lambda.a: A sticky note with one instruction, instead of a page in the manual.

layer.d: One round of the model’s moves — look around, then think. Layers are stacked.

layernorm.d: Rescales each vector to mean 0 and spread 1, then applies a learned scale and shift. It keeps the numbers in a steady range as they pass through many layers.
layernorm.a: Re-tuning every instrument to the same pitch before the next piece.

letterbox.d: Shrinking a picture to fit a frame of a different shape without stretching it, and filling the leftover bands with a plain colour.

linear.d: A learned matrix and a bias: every output number is a weighted sum of all the inputs, plus a constant. nn.Linear(a, b) has a × b weights and b biases.
linear.a: A mixing desk: every output channel is its own mix of all the input channels.

list.d: An ordered, changeable sequence: [a, b, c], read by position from 0.

logits.d: Raw scores, one per class, before softmax. The larger one wins; softmax turns them into probabilities if needed.
logits.a: Votes counted before they are turned into percentages.

loss.d: How surprised the model was by the right answer. Training makes it smaller.

lr-schedule.d: The learning rate changes over training: here it climbs from almost 0 (warmup), then falls along a cosine curve to 0, so early steps are gentle and the end settles.
lr-schedule.a: Pulling away slowly, cruising, then braking smoothly into the parking space.

mask.d: A grid as big as the picture saying which pixels belong to what — here 0 for background and a number for each person. (In the text model a mask said which words may look at which.)

matmul.d: Every row of the left matrix against every column of the right one: each pair gives one number, a sum of products. Q @ K.T gives every query against every key.
matmul.a: Comparing every applicant with every job description and writing down a score for each pair.

matplotlib.d: Python’s plotting library: plt.subplots makes a grid of panels, imshow draws a picture or a grid of numbers in one of them.

nn-module.d: The base of every PyTorch model part. A class that inherits from it gets its parameters tracked automatically, can be moved with .to(), switched between train() and eval(), saved with state_dict(), and is called like a function: layer(x) runs forward(x).
nn-module.a: A standard socket: anything built to it plugs into everything else.

no-grad.d: Inside it, PyTorch does not record operations for gradients: less memory and faster, for code that only uses the model.
no-grad.a: Doing a calculation in pen without keeping the working.

normalise.d: Subtracting each colour channel’s mean and dividing by its spread, so the model sees numbers around 0 with a spread of about 1 whatever the lighting.
normalise.a: Converting prices from different currencies into one before comparing them.

optimizer.d: The part of training that turns the gradients into changes of the weights — AdamW, Muon.

overfitting.d: Learning the training examples by heart instead of the pattern behind them.

padding.d: The part of a picture with no photo behind it: the bars around a photo that is shrunk to fit, or the border of a zoomed-out training picture. Its pixels are labelled 255, so they count in no loss and no score.

parameter.d: One number the model learns. Vision v1.5 has 1,308,706 of them (v1: 928,898).

parameter-tensor.d: A tensor marked as something the model learns: it shows up in model.parameters(), the optimizer updates it, and it is saved with the model.
parameter-tensor.a: A dial on the machine, as opposed to a reading on its display.

patch.d: A small square of the picture, here 8 × 8 pixels, that the model treats as one piece.

path.d: os.path.join(folder, name) builds a path with the right separator for the computer, so the same code works on macOS, Windows and Linux.
path.a: Writing an address in the local format.

pil.d: Python’s image library: opens photos, resizes them, draws shapes on them.

pixel accuracy.d: The share of all pixels that got the right class. Easy to fool: a picture that is mostly background gets a high score from a model that only ever says background.

point-in-polygon.d: The crossing rule: from the point, go straight to the right and count the outline’s edges you cross. An odd count means the point is inside.
point-in-polygon.a: Walking out of a fenced field in a straight line: if you crossed the fence an odd number of times, you started inside.

pointer-events.d: One set of events for mouse, pen and touch: pointerdown, pointermove, pointerup. setPointerCapture keeps sending the moves to the canvas even when the pointer leaves it mid-drag.
pointer-events.a: Holding on to the rope: until you let go, every tug comes to you.

polygon.d: A shape given by its corner points, joined by straight lines. An outline traced around a person is one.

polygon-fill.d: ImageDraw.polygon(points, fill=k) paints every pixel inside the outline with the value k. Drawn back to front, a later person covers an earlier one where they overlap.
polygon-fill.a: Colouring inside the lines, front figure last.

position.d: Where a token sits in its sentence: 0, 1, 2, …

query.d: What a patch is looking for. It is compared with every other patch’s key.

receptive field.d: The pixels one output of a layer is computed from. A v1.5 patch vector’s is 15 × 15 pixels.

residual.d: x = x + layer(x): each layer adds its result to what was there instead of replacing it, so information and gradients can always flow straight through.
residual.a: Annotating a document in the margin instead of rewriting it.

seed.d: torch.manual_seed(n) fixes the starting point of PyTorch’s random numbers, so every run makes the same “random” choices: the same weights, the same pictures, the same results.
seed.a: Shuffling a deck in exactly the same way every time, so the game can be replayed.

segment-distance.d: The nearest point of an edge to the pointer: project the pointer onto the edge’s line (t = how far along, from 0 to 1), keep t between the two ends, measure to it.
segment-distance.a: Dropping a plumb line onto a fence, and if it misses the fence, measuring to the nearest post.

segmentation mask.d: A grid as big as the picture holding one class per pixel — the answer, or the model’s guess at it.

self.d: Inside a method, self is the object the method was called on. self.x = … stores x on that object, so every other method can read it.
self.a: Writing “mine” on something so you can find it later.

self-attention.d: Attention within one set: every patch’s query against every patch’s key — the encoder’s attention.

semantic segmentation.d: Giving every pixel of a picture a class: what the pixel is part of. Here the classes are person and background.

shape.d: How many numbers a tensor has along each axis, e.g. (batch, channels, height, width). Most mistakes in model code are shape mistakes, so the notes give the shape of every tensor.
shape.a: The dimensions of a box: how many rows, how many columns, how many layers.

slicing.d: x[a:b] takes positions a up to (not including) b; x[:, a:] does it on the second axis of an array; a missing end means “to the end”. x[None] adds a new axis of size 1 in front.
slicing.a: Cutting a slice from a loaf without touching the rest.

softmax.d: Turns any list of scores into shares that are all positive and add up to 1: bigger scores get bigger shares, and the gaps between scores decide how much bigger.
softmax.a: Splitting a prize in proportion to how each contestant scored — exaggerated in favour of the best.

state-dict.d: A dict of every learned tensor of a model, by name. Saved with torch.save, loaded with load_state_dict, it rebuilds the trained model exactly.

stride.d: How far a convolution’s window moves at each step. Stride 2 halves the picture’s width and height.

super-init.d: Runs the parent class’s setup (here nn.Module’s) before the class adds its own parts — without it PyTorch cannot track the parameters.
super-init.a: Laying the foundation before building the walls.

tensor.d: PyTorch’s array: a grid of numbers with any number of axes, which can live on the GPU and remember how it was computed so gradients can flow back through it.
tensor.a: A spreadsheet that can have more than two dimensions and can do its sums on the graphics card.

train-eval.d: model.train() switches dropout on; model.eval() switches it off so the same input always gives the same output. They change behaviour, not weights.

training.d: Showing the model examples with their answers and nudging its parameters after each.

traitlets.d: Attributes declared on the class with .tag(sync=True) are copied between Python and the browser whenever either side changes them: self.people = … in Python, model.get('people') in JavaScript.
traitlets.a: A shared whiteboard both sides can read and write.

transpose.d: Swaps two axes: x.transpose(1, 2) turns (B, heads, patches, d) into (B, patches, heads, d). The numbers stay; how they are read changes.
transpose.a: Turning a table on its side.

try-except.d: Runs the try block; if a named error happens there, Python runs the except block instead of stopping the notebook.
try-except.a: A safety net under the trapeze.

tuple-unpacking.d: Assigns several names at once from a tuple or list: a, b = 1, 2. The right side is built first, then taken apart into the names on the left.
tuple-unpacking.a: Unpacking a parcel and putting each item on its own shelf.

undo-stack.d: Before each change, the current state is pushed onto a list (as JSON text). Undo takes the last one off and puts it back.
undo-stack.a: Keeping a copy of the page before every edit, and going back one copy at a time.

upsampling.d: Making a grid bigger: here the 24 × 36 patch scores are stretched to the 192 × 288 pixels.

validation.d: Checking the model on examples kept aside, to see if it learned the pattern rather than the examples.

value.d: What a patch hands over when a query matches its key.

vector.d: A list of numbers. Every patch becomes a vector of 128 numbers.

view.d: Reads the same numbers with a different shape — no copying. view(-1, 1, 1) makes a list of three into a (3, 1, 1) tensor; -1 means “whatever size makes it fit”.
view.a: Rearranging the same eggs from a 2 × 6 box into a 3 × 4 box.

view-transform.d: Every point is kept in the photo’s own pixels; the screen position is photo × view.s + (view.ox, view.oy). Zooming changes s, panning changes the offset — the outlines themselves never move.
view-transform.a: A camera over a map: moving or zooming the camera never moves the cities.

warmup.d: The first steps of training, during which the learning rate climbs from almost 0 to its full value, so the first, still random updates stay small.

weight-decay.d: Each step, every weight is shrunk a little towards 0, so the model prefers small weights unless large ones really help.
weight-decay.a: A small tax on every weight it holds.

with.d: Runs a block inside a context that is set up first and always undone afterwards — with torch.no_grad(): switches gradient tracking off for the block, then back on.
with.a: Borrowing a key that is handed back the moment you leave the room.

zero-grad.d: Clears the gradients left by the last step. PyTorch adds new gradients to old ones, so without this every step would push with all the previous steps’ gradients too.
zero-grad.a: Wiping the whiteboard before the next sum.
